summary: This component renders an interactive terminal display with optional typewriter animation and copy-to-clipboard functionality. It processes children to substitute variable values, animates command-line text character-by-character while revealing output lines whole, and lets users copy either all content or just the executable commands. The animation only starts when the terminal scrolls into view to avoid wasting effort on off-screen content.

explanations.39: The separator parameter defaults to a newline character, but callers can override it (like passing an empty string for Fragment children to avoid spurious line breaks).
explanations.42: If children is an array, we recursively process each item and join them with the separator, adding the separator between items but not after the last one.
explanations.52: We cast the child object to a ReactElement to access its type and props safely.
explanations.54: We look up the element's type (like the h1 function reference) in our headingPrefixMap to find its markdown prefix, falling back to an empty string if not found.
explanations.56: Fragment elements get an empty string separator so their text doesn't get spurious line breaks, while other elements use newlines.
explanations.65: This function returns different animation speeds depending on content length—longer terminals animate faster so the whole thing doesn't take forever.
explanations.113: The resolve function retrieves current variable values from a context store so we can substitute placeholders like %%name=default%% with actual values.
explanations.125: We build a Map keyed by the actual MDX heading component references (which are function objects, not strings) so we can later recover the markdown prefix (like '## ') that MDX strips away.
explanations.139: We process children once to replace all variable placeholders with their resolved values, wrapping substituted values in VarToken components for styling.
explanations.152: We capture the animation line list exactly once when typewriter mode is toggled on, so if the user edits a variable during animation, the in-flight animation finishes with the original text.
explanations.159: We calculate effective speeds by first checking if the user provided explicit props, and if not, we auto-scale based on how many lines there are.
explanations.170: We set up an IntersectionObserver to detect when the terminal scrolls into view, so we only start the expensive typewriter animation for visible terminals.
explanations.178: IntersectionObserver lets us watch when the DOM element enters the viewport; we check at 10% visibility threshold.
explanations.207: This regex test checks if the line starts with optional whitespace followed by $ or #, which indicates it's a command line (not output).
explanations.209: We only animate command lines character-by-character; output lines appear instantly in the next step.
explanations.215: Empty lines get an 80ms pause; other lines get the configured delay before we move to the next line.
explanations.240: After extracting text to copy, if copyCommandOnly is true, we filter to only command lines and strip their prompts so the result is directly pasteable into a shell.
explanations.265: animDisplay shows either nothing (if animation is done), or the partially-typed current line joined with fully-revealed previous lines.
explanations.266: We slice the current line to show only the characters we've typed so far, or an empty string if we haven't reached this line yet.
explanations.277: During animation we show a pointer cursor to hint that the user can click to skip.
explanations.310: The ghost span renders the complete final content invisibly so the <pre> reserves the full height immediately, preventing the page from reflowing as each line animates in.
